title: Your Gut May Affect Your Response to Stress — Study
paragraphs: Many studies have shown that stress can affect your gut. People going through stressful periods often report stomach problems, and there's also a link between trauma and developing conditions like irritable bowel syndrome at a later stage in life.
However, researchers in Germany and Austria believe the brain-gut connection could go both ways.

The gut is home to trillions of tiny organisms that create an environment inside your body known as the gut microbiome. And new research suggests that these organisms may play a role in how our bodies respond to stress.
The researchers looked at the gut bacteria of 74 healthy adults. The participants were then put in either a stressful situation or a non-stressful control condition.
In the stressful situation, they had to do difficult math problems while they were repeatedly interrupted and told their performance wasn't good enough.
The researchers measured stress levels by checking the participants' saliva for cortisol, a hormone linked to stress. Participants also gave reports on how stressed they felt.
The results showed that people with a greater variety of gut bacteria often reported higher levels of stress. Their cortisol levels also increased faster when in the stressful situation.

Study author Thomas Karner explained that the gut and brain are always communicating, and the study suggests that people with a more varied gut microbiome may have a stronger response to stressful situations.
This isn't necessarily a bad thing — it could actually help in situations involving an immediate challenge.

A more varied gut microbiome could mean someone is better able to adjust their response to stress depending on the situation — and they may use their strong response to focus on and deal with the source of their stress, Karner said.
Of course, there are many other things that shape how people respond to stress — genetics, life experiences, personality and more.
However, while the scientists said that more research is needed, this study offers an interesting new look at the connection between the gut microbiome and the brain.
